claim: Rif1 is a large multifaceted protein involved in various processes of DNA metabolism – from telomere length regulation and replication to double-strand break repair.
source: Rif1 is a large multifaceted protein involved in various processes of DNA metabolism – from telomere length regulation and replication to double-strand break repair.
evidence: This is a general statement about Rif1 function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: H. polymorpha Rif1 suppresses telomerase-dependent telomere elongation.
source: We show that, similar to other yeast species, H. polymorpha Rif1 suppresses telomerase-dependent telomere elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C demonstrating telomere elongation in Δrif1 strains and dependence on telomerase.

claim: H. polymorpha Rif1 is recruited at telomeres via direct DNA binding.
source: We uncover two novel modes of Rif1 recruitment at H. polymorpha telomeres: via direct DNA binding and through the association with the Ku heterodimer.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data showing DNA binding (Figure 3) and ChIP data showing telomeric localization (Figure 1D, Figure 4).

claim: H. polymorpha Rif1 is recruited at telomeres through association with the Ku heterodimer.
source: We uncover two novel modes of Rif1 recruitment at H. polymorpha telomeres: via direct DNA binding and through the association with the Ku heterodimer.
evidence: This is supported by Y2H data (Figure 5A), Co-IP data (Figure 5D), and ChIP showing reduced Rif1 binding in Ku deletion strains (Figure 5E).

claim: Both modes of Rif1 recruitment at least partially require the intrinsically disordered N-terminal extension.
source: Both of these modes (at least partially) require the intrinsically disordered N-terminal extension – a region of the protein present exclusively in yeast species.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing reduced telomeric localization of Rif1ΔNTE (Figure 1D), biophysical characterization of NTE disorder (Figure 2), and DNA binding assays (Figure 3, Figure 4).

claim: The N-terminal extension of Rif1 is present exclusively in yeast species.
source: Both of these modes (at least partially) require the intrinsically disordered N-terminal extension – a region of the protein present exclusively in yeast species.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and comparison of Rif1 homologues across species (Supplementary file 1).

claim: Rif1 binds Stn1 in H. polymorpha.
source: We also demonstrate that Rif1 binds Stn1 and promotes its accumulation at telomeres in H. polymorpha.
evidence: This is supported by Y2H data (Figure 5A, Figure 6B, G) and Co-IP experiments (Figure 6A).

claim: Rif1 promotes Stn1 accumulation at telomeres in H. polymorpha.
source: We also demonstrate that Rif1 binds Stn1 and promotes its accumulation at telomeres in H. polymorpha.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing loss of Stn1 telomeric localization in Δrif1 strains (Figure 6F).

claim: Telomeres are essential for protection of chromosomes from degradation and fusions by the DNA repair machinery.
source: Chromosomes of most eukaryotic organisms end in distinctive nucleoprotein structures, called telomeres, which are essential for protection of chromosomes from degradation and fusions by the DNA repair machinery (de Lange, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Lange, 2018.

claim: Short G/C-rich telomeric DNA repeats provide a platform for loading of a specific set of telomeric proteins forming complex dynamic assemblies at the ends of the chromosomes.
source: Short G/C-rich telomeric DNA repeats provide a platform for loading of a specific set of telomeric proteins forming complex dynamic assemblies at the ends of the chromosomes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about telomere structure and function.

claim: Dividing cells are constantly losing telomeric repeats due to incomplete replication unless counteracted by either recombination or activity of the ribonucleoprotein complex telomerase.
source: Dividing cells are constantly losing telomeric repeats due to incomplete replication unless counteracted by either recombination or activity of the ribonucleoprotein complex telomerase.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the end-replication problem and telomere maintenance mechanisms.

claim: Replenishing of telomeric DNA by telomerase is crucial for long-term proliferation of the majority of eukaryotic cell types.
source: Replenishing of telomeric DNA by telomerase is crucial for long-term proliferation of the majority of eukaryotic cell types.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about telomerase function in cell proliferation.

claim: Many positive and negative regulators of telomerase have been identified, many of which are components of the telomeric chromatin.
source: This process is highly coordinated, and plenty of positive and negative regulators of telomerase have been identified to date, many of which are components of the telomeric chromatin (Lee et al., 2021; Lim and Cech, 2021; Shay and Wright, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2021; Lim and Cech, 2021; Shay and Wright, 2019.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, the double-stranded portion of telomeres is bound by Rap1 through its duplicated MYB domain.
source: In budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the double-stranded portion of telomeres is bound by Rap1 through its duplicated MYB domain (Henry et al., 1990; Shore and Nasmyth, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Henry et al., 1990; Shore and Nasmyth, 1987.

claim: Rif1 and Rif2 are recruited to telomeres via interaction with Rap1 C-terminus (RCT) in S. cerevisiae.
source: Two additional telomeric proteins – Rif1 and Rif2 – are recruited to telomeres via interaction with Rap1 C-terminus (RCT) (Hardy et al., 1992; Wotton and Shore, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hardy et al., 1992; Wotton and Shore, 1997.

claim: Both Rif1 and Rif2 restrict telomerase action in S. cerevisiae.
source: Both of them restrict telomerase action and their double deletion (as well as deletion of the RCT) leads to telomere hyperelongation (Teng et al., 2000; Wotton and Shore, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Teng et al., 2000; Wotton and Shore, 1997.

claim: Double deletion of Rif1 and Rif2 leads to telomere hyperelongation in S. cerevisiae.
source: Both of them restrict telomerase action and their double deletion (as well as deletion of the RCT) leads to telomere hyperelongation (Teng et al., 2000; Wotton and Shore, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Teng et al., 2000; Wotton and Shore, 1997.

claim: Rap1 recruits the histone deacetylase complex Sir2/Sir3/Sir4 through an interaction between Sir4 and RCT in S. cerevisiae.
source: Rap1 also recruits the histone deacetylase complex Sir2/Sir3/Sir4 (through an interaction between Sir4 and RCT) providing the basis for the silencing of telomere-proximal genes (Moretti et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moretti et al., 1994.

claim: The C-terminal portion of Rif1 contains a Rap1-binding motif (Rif1RBM) and a tetramerization module (Rif1CTD).
source: The C-terminal portion of Rif1 contains a Rap1-binding motif (Rif1RBM) and a tetramerization module (Rif1CTD), while Rif2 contains two Rap1-binding sites, therefore Rap1/Rif1/Rif2 can form complex DNA-protein structures at the chromosome ends, inhibiting both telomerase recruitment and telomere silencing (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2013.

claim: Rif2 contains two Rap1-binding sites in S. cerevisiae.
source: The C-terminal portion of Rif1 contains a Rap1-binding motif (Rif1RBM) and a tetramerization module (Rif1CTD), while Rif2 contains two Rap1-binding sites, therefore Rap1/Rif1/Rif2 can form complex DNA-protein structures at the chromosome ends, inhibiting both telomerase recruitment and telomere silencing (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2013.

claim: Rap1/Rif1/Rif2 can form complex DNA-protein structures at the chromosome ends, inhibiting both telomerase recruitment and telomere silencing.
source: The C-terminal portion of Rif1 contains a Rap1-binding motif (Rif1RBM) and a tetramerization module (Rif1CTD), while Rif2 contains two Rap1-binding sites, therefore Rap1/Rif1/Rif2 can form complex DNA-protein structures at the chromosome ends, inhibiting both telomerase recruitment and telomere silencing (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2013.

claim: Rif1 can localize at telomeres in a Rap1-independent fashion through its large HEAT repeats containing N-terminal domain (Rif1NTD) that exhibits strong affinity to DNA with some preference towards 3'-overhang containing ss-ds junctions.
source: In addition, Rif1 can localize at telomeres in a Rap1-independent fashion through its large HEAT repeats containing N-terminal domain (Rif1NTD) that exhibits strong affinity to DNA with some preference towards 3'-overhang containing ss-ds junctions (Mattarocci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mattarocci et al., 2017.

claim: DNA binding by Rif1NTD is important for telomerase regulation and attenuation of end resection at telomeres.
source: This binding mode is important for telomerase regulation and attenuation of end resection at telomeres.
evidence: This is based on inference from the cited work (Mattarocci et al., 2017) about the functional importance of Rif1NTD DNA binding.

claim: ScRif1NTD was proposed to contain an interaction site for a yet unidentified protein partner at telomeres.
source: Recently, the ScRif1NTD was proposed to contain an interaction site for a yet unidentified protein partner at telomeres (Shubin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shubin et al., 2021.

claim: The single-stranded region of telomeres (3'-overhang) is bound and protected by the Cdc13 protein together with its partners Stn1 and Ten1 (the CST complex).
source: The single-stranded region of telomeres (3'-overhang) is bound and protected by the Cdc13 protein (Garvik et al., 1995; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Nugent et al., 1996) together with its partners Stn1 and Ten1 (the CST complex; Grandin et al., 2001; Grandin et al., 1997; Mersaoui and Wellinger, 2019; Wellinger and Zakian, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garvik et al., 1995; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Nugent et al., 1996; Grandin et al., 2001; Grandin et al., 1997; Mersaoui and Wellinger, 2019; Wellinger and Zakian, 2012.

claim: Cdc13 is a central hub for telomeric DNA synthesis as it mediates the main pathway of telomerase recruitment (synthesis of the G-strand), as well as assists in loading of the Polα (synthesis of the C-strand).
source: Cdc13 is a central hub for telomeric DNA synthesis as it mediates the main pathway of telomerase recruitment (synthesis of the G-strand), as well as assists in loading of the Polα(synthesis of the C-strand) (Qi and Zakian, 2000; Wellinger and Zakian, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Qi and Zakian, 2000; Wellinger and Zakian, 2012.

claim: Telomerase recruitment in S. cerevisiae depends on the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer (Ku).
source: Telomerase recruitment in S. cerevisiae also depends on another telomeric complex – the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer (Ku): it binds a stem-loop structure within telomerase RNA and the Sir4 protein at telomeres (Hass and Zappulla, 2015; Peterson et al., 2001; Stellwagen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hass and Zappulla, 2015; Peterson et al., 2001; Stellwagen et al., 2003.

claim: Ku binds a stem-loop structure within telomerase RNA and the Sir4 protein at telomeres in S. cerevisiae.
source: Telomerase recruitment in S. cerevisiae also depends on another telomeric complex – the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer (Ku): it binds a stem-loop structure within telomerase RNA and the Sir4 protein at telomeres (Hass and Zappulla, 2015; Peterson et al., 2001; Stellwagen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hass and Zappulla, 2015; Peterson et al., 2001; Stellwagen et al., 2003.

claim: Ku can bind DNA directly and apparently does so at sub-telomeric regions and, perhaps, at the ds-ss junction of the telomere.
source: In addition, Ku can bind DNA directly and apparently does so at sub-telomeric regions and, perhaps, at the ds-ss junction of the telomere (Larcher et al., 2016; Lopez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Larcher et al., 2016; Lopez et al., 2011.

claim: Ku loss leads to telomere shortening and Exo1-dependent accumulation of single-stranded telomeric DNA.
source: Ku loss leads to telomere shortening and Exo1-dependent accumulation of single-stranded telomeric DNA (Bonetti et al., 2010; Boulton and Jackson, 1996; Gravel et al., 1998; Polotnianka et al., 1998; Porter et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bonetti et al., 2010; Boulton and Jackson, 1996; Gravel et al., 1998; Polotnianka et al., 1998; Porter et al., 1996.

claim: Rap1 protein is a central transcription factor, controlling expression of hundreds of genes in budding yeast.
source: Rap1 protein is a central transcription factor, controlling expression of hundreds of genes in budding yeast (Azad and Tomar, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Azad and Tomar, 2016.

claim: A regulatory role during RNA PolII transcription was recently described for ScCST complex.
source: A regulatory role during RNA PolII transcription was recently described for ScCST complex (Calvo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Calvo et al., 2019.

claim: Ku heterodimer is a key component of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) machinery.
source: Ku heterodimer is a key component of the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) machinery (Frit et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frit et al., 2019.

claim: Rif1 protein binds Glc7 (PP1) phosphatase and this interaction is important for regulation of replication initiation at several origins.
source: Rif1 protein binds Glc7 (PP1) phosphatase and this interaction is important for regulation of replication initiation at several origins (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014), but not for telomere length control (Shubin and Greider, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014.

claim: The Rif1-Glc7 interaction is not important for telomere length control.
source: Rif1 protein binds Glc7 (PP1) phosphatase and this interaction is important for regulation of replication initiation at several origins (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014), but not for telomere length control (Shubin and Greider, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shubin and Greider, 2020.

claim: Rif1's function in replication, but not the telomeric role, is conserved among eukaryotic Rif1 homologues.
source: Interestingly, this function in replication, but not the telomeric role, is conserved among eukaryotic Rif1 homologues (see Alavi et al., 2021 for a recent review).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alavi et al., 2021.

claim: The only known species outside budding yeast clade which contains Rif1 as a component of 'normal' telomeric chromatin is fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: The only known species outside budding yeast clade which contains Rif1 as a component of 'normal' telomeric chromatin is fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, although SpRif1 is recruited through an interaction with Taz1 protein rather than Rap1 (Kanoh and Ishikawa, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kanoh and Ishikawa, 2001.

claim: SpRif1 is recruited through an interaction with Taz1 protein rather than Rap1.
source: The only known species outside budding yeast clade which contains Rif1 as a component of 'normal' telomeric chromatin is fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, although SpRif1 is recruited through an interaction with Taz1 protein rather than Rap1 (Kanoh and Ishikawa, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kanoh and Ishikawa, 2001.

claim: Mammalian Rif1 associates with dysfunctional telomeres (and other types of DSB) together with 53BP1.
source: Mammalian Rif1 associates with dysfunctional telomeres (and other types of DSB) together with 53BP1, limiting accumulation of ssDNA through a mechanism involving Rev7, the Shieldin complex, CST and Polα, and driving the DSB repair toward NHEJ (Barazas et al., 2018; Chapman et al., 2013; Dev et al., 2018; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2018; Mirman et al., 2018; Noordermeer et al., 2018; Tomida et al., 2018; Zimmermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barazas et al., 2018; Chapman et al., 2013; Dev et al., 2018; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2018; Mirman et al., 2018; Noordermeer et al., 2018; Tomida et al., 2018; Zimmermann et al., 2013.

claim: Mammalian Rif1 limits accumulation of ssDNA through a mechanism involving Rev7, the Shieldin complex, CST and Polα, and drives DSB repair toward NHEJ.
source: Mammalian Rif1 associates with dysfunctional telomeres (and other types of DSB) together with 53BP1, limiting accumulation of ssDNA through a mechanism involving Rev7, the Shieldin complex, CST and Polα, and driving the DSB repair toward NHEJ (Barazas et al., 2018; Chapman et al., 2013; Dev et al., 2018; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2018; Mirman et al., 2018; Noordermeer et al., 2018; Tomida et al., 2018; Zimmermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barazas et al., 2018; Chapman et al., 2013; Dev et al., 2018; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2018; Mirman et al., 2018; Noordermeer et al., 2018; Tomida et al., 2018; Zimmermann et al., 2013.

claim: S. cerevisiae Rif1 localizes to non-telomeric DSBs and promotes NHEJ through its DNA binding NTD.
source: Interestingly, S. cerevisiae Rif1 also localizes to non-telomeric DSBs and promotes NHEJ through its DNA binding NTD, suggesting that Rif1 may be a conserved NHEJ factor (Mattarocci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mattarocci et al., 2017.

claim: Rif1 may be a conserved NHEJ factor.
source: Interestingly, S. cerevisiae Rif1 also localizes to non-telomeric DSBs and promotes NHEJ through its DNA binding NTD, suggesting that Rif1 may be a conserved NHEJ factor (Mattarocci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation based on inference from the cited work (Mattarocci et al., 2017) and comparison with mammalian Rif1 function.

claim: H. polymorpha DL-1 is distantly related to S. cerevisiae.
source: The thermotolerant methylotrophic budding yeast species Hansenula polymorpha DL-1 is distantly related to S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the phylogenetic relationship between these yeast species.

claim: Rap1 has two paralogues in H. polymorpha (Rap1A and Rap1B) with distinct DNA recognition properties.
source: Rap1 has two paralogues in H. polymorpha (Rap1A and Rap1B) with distinct DNA recognition properties (Malyavko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Malyavko et al., 2019.

claim: HpRap1A is located at the subtelomeric regions with no reported telomeric role.
source: HpRap1A is located at the subtelomeric regions with no reported telomeric role.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors (Malyavko et al., 2019).

claim: HpRap1B is the major telomeric dsDNA binder with the ability to control telomere length.
source: HpRap1B is the major telomeric dsDNA binder with the ability to control telomere length, although the primary target of its inhibition appears to be recombination rather than telomerase (Malyavko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Malyavko et al., 2019.

claim: The primary target of HpRap1B's inhibition appears to be recombination rather than telomerase.
source: HpRap1B is the major telomeric dsDNA binder with the ability to control telomere length, although the primary target of its inhibition appears to be recombination rather than telomerase (Malyavko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Malyavko et al., 2019.

claim: The RIF2 gene is absent from H. polymorpha genome (and other yeasts outside Saccharomycetaceae family).
source: The RIF2 gene is absent from H. polymorpha genome (and other yeasts outside Saccharomycetaceae family).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and comparison across yeast species.

claim: A shorter version of Cdc13 protein is present in H. polymorpha, which possesses strong affinity for telomeric G-strand in vitro and binds Stn1 protein.
source: A shorter version of Cdc13 protein is present in H. polymorpha, which possesses strong affinity for telomeric G-strand in vitro and binds Stn1 protein (Malyavko and Dontsova, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Malyavko and Dontsova, 2020.

claim: HpCdc13 interacts with HpTERT in the yeast-two-hybrid (Y2H) assay.
source: HpCdc13 also interacts with HpTERT in the yeast-two-hybrid (Y2H) assay.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors (Malyavko and Dontsova, 2020).

claim: Amino acid sequence similarity between ScRif1 and HpRif1 is very low (16% identity).
source: Amino acid sequence similarity between ScRif1 and HpRif1 is very low (16% identity); however, alignment of multiple budding yeast homologues revealed several conserved elements within HpRif1 (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1): the RVxF/SILK motif (residues 277–306), the N-terminal HEAT repeats containing domain (Rif1NTD, residues ~ 310–1000) and the C-terminal domain (Rif1CTD, residues ~ 1475–1521).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Alignment of multiple budding yeast homologues revealed several conserved elements within HpRif1: the RVxF/SILK motif (residues 277–306), the N-terminal HEAT repeats containing domain (Rif1NTD, residues ~ 310–1000) and the C-terminal domain (Rif1CTD, residues ~ 1475–1521).
source: Amino acid sequence similarity between ScRif1 and HpRif1 is very low (16% identity); however, alignment of multiple budding yeast homologues revealed several conserved elements within HpRif1 (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1): the RVxF/SILK motif (residues 277–306), the N-terminal HEAT repeats containing domain (Rif1NTD, residues ~ 310–1000) and the C-terminal domain (Rif1CTD, residues ~ 1475–1521).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: HpRif1 contains large potentially disordered regions (residues ~ 1000–1475 and 1–277).
source: HpRif1 also contains large potentially disordered regions (residues ~ 1000–1475 and 1–277).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction and sequence analysis.

claim: Deletion of the RIF1 gene in H. polymorpha leads to markedly elongated telomeres.
source: We observed markedly elongated telomeres in the Δrif1 strain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Concomitant deletion of the RAD52 gene did not influence telomere overelongation in the Δrif1 strain.
source: Concomitant deletion of the RAD52 gene did not influence telomere overelongation in the Δrif1 strain, whereas deletion of telomerase RNA gene (TER) led to telomere shortening (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of telomerase RNA gene (TER) led to telomere shortening in the Δrif1 strain.
source: Concomitant deletion of the RAD52 gene did not influence telomere overelongation in the Δrif1 strain, whereas deletion of telomerase RNA gene (TER) led to telomere shortening (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Δrif1Δter double knock-out strain senesced upon continuous propagation, with no substantial increase in survival compared to the Δter strain.
source: The Δrif1Δter double knock-out strain senesced upon continuous propagation, with no substantial increase in survival compared to the Δter strain (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The more likely target of Rif1's inhibition is telomerase, and not the recombination pathway of telomere elongation.
source: These observations suggest that the more likely target of Rif1's inhibition is telomerase, and not the recombination pathway of telomere elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing telomerase-dependent telomere elongation in Δrif1 strains (Figure 1B, C).

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitated from the RIF1-HA strain via anti-HA antibodies was enriched with telomere proximal fragment 'TEL' compared to the internal fragment 'ALA1'.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitated from this strain via anti-HA antibodies was enriched with telomere proximal fragment 'TEL' compared to the internal fragment 'ALA1', suggesting that Rif1 localizes at H. polymorpha telomeres in vivo (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Rif1 localizes at H. polymorpha telomeres in vivo.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitated from this strain via anti-HA antibodies was enriched with telomere proximal fragment 'TEL' compared to the internal fragment 'ALA1', suggesting that Rif1 localizes at H. polymorpha telomeres in vivo (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Rif1 is a telomeric protein inhibiting telomerase action in H. polymorpha similar to its S. cerevisiae homologue.
source: Thus, Rif1 is a telomeric protein inhibiting telomerase action in H. polymorpha similar to its S. cerevisiae homologue.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented (Figure 1B-D) and comparison with known S. cerevisiae Rif1 function.

claim: Telomeric localization of ScRif1 is largely dependent on the interaction with ScRap1.
source: Telomeric localization of ScRif1 is largely dependent on the interaction with ScRap1, and mutation in the Rif1RBM, located within the C-terminal part of the protein, greatly reduce the amount of telomere-bound ScRif1 (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2013.

claim: Mutation in the Rif1RBM, located within the C-terminal part of the protein, greatly reduce the amount of telomere-bound ScRif1.
source: Telomeric localization of ScRif1 is largely dependent on the interaction with ScRap1, and mutation in the Rif1RBM, located within the C-terminal part of the protein, greatly reduce the amount of telomere-bound ScRif1 (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2013.

claim: A similar Rap1-binding motif could not be found in the HpRif1 sequence.
source: We could not find a similar Rap1-binding motif in the HpRif1 sequence (Supplementary file 1), suggesting that HpRif1 may be recruited at telomeres in a Rap1-independent fashion, or such RBM is located in a different region of the protein.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: HpRif1 may be recruited at telomeres in a Rap1-independent fashion, or such RBM is located in a different region of the protein.
source: We could not find a similar Rap1-binding motif in the HpRif1 sequence (Supplementary file 1), suggesting that HpRif1 may be recruited at telomeres in a Rap1-independent fashion, or such RBM is located in a different region of the protein.
evidence: This is speculation based on the absence of a conserved Rap1-binding motif in HpRif1.

claim: Phenotypic consequences of the ScRif1 loss or removal of the C-terminal domain of ScRap1 are similar, as they both result in the telomerase-dependent telomere overelongation.
source: Phenotypic consequences of the ScRif1 loss or removal of the C-terminal domain of ScRap1 are similar, as they both result in the telomerase-dependent telomere overelongation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about S. cerevisiae telomere biology.

claim: Elongation of telomeres in the B1–526 strain (expressing C-terminally truncated Rap1B) is largely Rad52-dependent.
source: However, we have previously found that elongation of telomeres in the B1–526 strain (expressing C-terminally truncated Rap1B) is largely Rad52-dependent, providing further indication for a Rap1-independent Rif1 function.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors (Malyavko et al., 2019).

claim: If Rap1B is not involved in Rif1 recruitment – then Rif1 should not bind to double stranded telomeric DNA.
source: If Rap1B is not involved in Rif1 recruitment – then Rif1 should not bind to double stranded telomeric DNA.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the assumption that Rap1B is the primary dsDNA binding factor at telomeres.

claim: Rap1B binds telomeric repeats with similar efficiency at the internal locus or at the chromosome end (only ~2 fold difference between WSC3 and TEL signals for the intTEL18 strain).
source: As expected, Rap1B binds telomeric repeats with similar efficiency at the internal locus or at the chromosome end (only ~2 fold difference between WSC3 and TEL signals for the intTEL18 strain, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rif1 association with the internal telomeric repeats is weak and close to the background levels (ChIP WSC3 signal is ~8 fold lower than TEL).
source: On the contrary, Rif1 association with the internal telomeric repeats is weak and close to the background levels (ChIP WSC3 signal is ~8 fold lower than TEL, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Interaction with Rap1 is not a major determinant of telomeric localization of Rif1 in H. polymorpha.
source: Therefore, we conclude that interaction with Rap1 is not a major determinant of telomeric localization of Rif1 in H. polymorpha.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChIP data showing differential binding of Rap1B and Rif1 to internal vs. terminal telomeric repeats (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).

claim: The Rif1NTE1-264 fragment can be efficiently recruited to telomeres.
source: Quite unexpectedly, we found that this Rif1NTE1-264 fragment can be efficiently recruited to telomeres, according to our ChIP experiments (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Removal of residues 1–264 from HpRif1 (Rif1∆NTE) strongly reduced its ability to associate with telomeric DNA.
source: Moreover, removal of residues 1–264 from HpRif1 (Rif1∆NTE) strongly reduced its ability to associate with telomeric DNA (Figure 1D), and led to telomere elongation (Figure 1E), while having no effect on the accumulation of the protein (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data (Figure 1D), Southern blot data (Figure 1E), and Western blot data (Figure 1F).

claim: Removal of residues 1–264 from HpRif1 (Rif1∆NTE) led to telomere elongation.
source: Moreover, removal of residues 1–264 from HpRif1 (Rif1∆NTE) strongly reduced its ability to associate with telomeric DNA (Figure 1D), and led to telomere elongation (Figure 1E), while having no effect on the accumulation of the protein (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Removal of residues 1–264 from HpRif1 (Rif1∆NTE) had no effect on the accumulation of the protein.

claim: Rif1NTE1-264 is an important determinant of Rif1 telomeric localization in H. polymorpha.

claim: N-terminal extensions of Rif1 homologues from distantly related budding yeasts have no significant similarity.

claim: Rif1 NTE may not have any conserved folding.
source: Multiple protein sequence alignment of Rif1 homologues from distantly related budding yeasts revealed that N-terminal extensions have no significant similarity (Supplementary file 1), suggesting that Rif1 NTE may not have any conserved folding.

claim: MetaDisorder prediction for 1–264 fragment of HpRif1 suggests that it lacks any secondary structure.

claim: HpRif1NTE may be unstructured or intrinsically disordered.
source: Moreover, MetaDisorder prediction (Kozlowski and Bujnicki, 2012) for 1–264 fragment of HpRif1 suggests that it lacks any secondary structure (Figure 2A), that is HpRif1NTE may be unstructured or intrinsically disordered.
evidence: This is speculation based on computational prediction (Figure 2A) and is later confirmed experimentally (Figure 2D, E).

claim: During gel-filtration and denaturing gel electrophoresis 28 kDa Rif1NTE1-264 behaves like a protein with higher molecular weight.

claim: Aberrant migration during gel-filtration and denaturing gel electrophoresis is common for many intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs).
source: It is worth noting that during gel-filtration and denaturing gel electrophoresis 28 kDa Rif1NTE1-264 behaves like a protein with higher molecular weight (Figure 2B and C), which is common for many intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) (Tompa, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tompa, 2002.

claim: Circular dichroism spectra of Rif1NTE1-264 recorded at different temperatures demonstrated that it contains no significant α-helical or β-strand secondary structural elements over this temperature range.

claim: The isoelliptical point near 210 nm in CD spectra is indicative of the equilibrium between left-handed PPII and truly unordered conformation, which has been often observed in CD spectra of IDPs.

evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: DNA binding by Rif1 has been demonstrated in several species (including mammals, fission, and budding yeasts).
source: DNA binding by Rif1 has been demonstrated in several species (including mammals, fission, and budding yeasts; Kanoh et al., 2015; Mattarocci et al., 2017; Moriyama et al., 2018; Sukackaite et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanoh et al., 2015; Mattarocci et al., 2017; Moriyama et al., 2018; Sukackaite et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2010.

claim: Only two HpRif1 fragments (both containing amino acids 1–264) could bind telomeric DNA (both single- and double-stranded).
source: We found that only two fragments (both containing amino acids 1–264 of HpRif1) could bind telomeric DNA (both single- and double-stranded, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HpRif1 contains a DNA-binding domain at its N-terminus.
source: Thus, HpRif1 contains a DNA-binding domain at its N-terminus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on EMSA data (Figure 3C).

claim: Affinities of Rif1NTE1-264 for telomeric ssDNA and dsDNA are very close (Kdapp ~ 240 nM for FAM-Tel4(G), and Kdapp ~ 430 nM for FAM-Tel4(GC)).
source: The titration experiments revealed that affinities for telomeric ssDNA and dsDNA are very close (Kdapp ~ 240 nM for FAM-Tel4(G), and Kdapp ~ 430 nM for FAM-Tel4(GC)) in our experimental conditions (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EMSA data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rif1NTE1-264 poorly differentiates between Tel4(G), Tel4(C) (C-rich telomeric strand) and Tel4(GC) oligonucleotides.
source: The competition EMSA confirmed that Rif1NTE1-264 poorly differentiates between Tel4(G), Tel4(C) (C-rich telomeric strand) and Tel4(GC) oligonucleotides (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by competition EMSA data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rif1NTE1-264 has some preference towards telomeric substrates compared with the G/C-poor DNA oligonucleotides.
source: However, it also revealed that Rif1NTE1-264 has some preference towards telomeric substrates compared with the G/C-poor DNA oligonucleotides (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by competition EMSA data shown in Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and Table 1.

claim: Amino acids 101–264 of HpRif1 are dispensable for DNA-binding activity.
source: We tested several NTE truncation constructs for their ability to shift telomeric DNA in vitro and found amino acids 101–264 to be dispensable for DNA-binding activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Region 1–100 of HpRif1 contains two similar clusters enriched in positively charged residues (38KRNNRSR44 and 79KRSTNNKSK87).
source: Then we noticed that region 1–100 of HpRif1 contains two similar clusters enriched in positively charged residues (38KRNNRSR44 and 79KRSTNNKSK87, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 8ARif1NTE1-264 (with eight alanine substitutions in both clusters) retained little (if any) ability to bind DNA in vitro.
source: According to the results of the EMSA experiments, 8ARif1NTE1-264 retained little (if any) ability to bind DNA in vitro (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Regions 38–44 and 79–87 are crucial elements of DNA-binding activity of Rif1NTE1-264 in vitro.
source: Thus, we conclude that regions 38–44 and 79–87 are crucial elements of DNA-binding activity of Rif1NTE1-264 in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on EMSA data with mutant proteins (Figure 4C).

claim: Even four alanine substitutions (in either motif) reduce HpRif1 association with telomere VII to the background levels.
source: Even four alanine substitutions (in either motif) reduce HpRif1 association with telomere VII to the background levels (Figure 4D), while having little effect on the protein abundance (Figure 4E).

claim: Four alanine substitutions in either motif have little effect on HpRif1 protein abundance.
source: Even four alanine substitutions (in either motif) reduce HpRif1 association with telomere VII to the background levels (Figure 4D), while having little effect on the protein abundance (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Telomeres in all three mutant strains (4A1, 4A2, 8A) were elongated, and comparable to the Rif1∆NTE strain.
source: Telomeres in all three mutant strains were elongated, and comparable to the Rif1∆NTE strain (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: DNA-binding activity of the N-terminal extension helps to recruit HpRif1 to telomeres.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate an important role of regions 38–44 and 79–87 for HpRif1 function and argue that DNA-binding activity of the N-terminal extension helps to recruit HpRif1 to telomeres.

claim: ScRif1 binds DNA in vitro via its crook-shaped structural NTD.
source: ScRif1 binds DNA in vitro via its crook-shaped structural NTD, however we did not observe DNA binding activity of the HpRif1 fragments corresponding to this region of the protein (Figure 3).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ScRif1 from previous studies.

claim: HpRif1 fragments corresponding to the NTD region did not show DNA binding activity.
source: ScRif1 binds DNA in vitro via its crook-shaped structural NTD, however we did not observe DNA binding activity of the HpRif1 fragments corresponding to this region of the protein (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: According to the published ScRif1NTD/DNA structure, 19 charged residues have the potential to contact the DNA backbone.
source: According to the published ScRif1NTD/DNA structure, 19 charged residues have the potential to contact the DNA backbone (Mattarocci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mattarocci et al., 2017.

claim: Of 19 charged residues in ScRif1NTD that potentially contact DNA, only four are conserved in H. polymorpha Rif1.
source: Of these 19, only four are conserved in H. polymorpha Rif1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Double mutant HpRif1K658E/K666E is expressed at considerably lower levels than WT HpRif1.
source: Double mutant HpRif1K658E/K666E is expressed at considerably lower levels than WT HpRif1, indicating that residues K658 and K666 are important for protein stability (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Residues K658 and K666 are important for HpRif1 protein stability.
source: Double mutant HpRif1K658E/K666E is expressed at considerably lower levels than WT HpRif1, indicating that residues K658 and K666 are important for protein stability (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced protein levels observed in the mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Substitution of K504 and R539 for glutamines does not lead to detectable changes in Rif1 telomere occupancy or telomere length.
source: Substitution of the other two conserved amino acids (K504 and R539) for glutamines does not lead to detectable changes in Rif1 telomere occupancy or telomere length (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) and Southern blot data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).

claim: HpRif1 may lack the DNA-binding mode described for ScRif1 or it utilizes different amino acids for such interaction.
source: Thus, HpRif1 may lack the DNA-binding mode described for ScRif1 or it utilizes different amino acids for such interaction.
evidence: This is speculation based on the lack of conservation of DNA-contacting residues and the negative results from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Y2H analysis revealed two Rif1-interacting partners: Ku80 and Stn1.
source: Rif1 and several other telomeric proteins were tested in yeast-two-hybrid (Y2H) assay, which revealed two Rif1-interacting partners: Ku80 and Stn1 (Figure 5A).

claim: The interaction with Ku80 (but not with Stn1) appears to be mediated through the Rif1NTE1-264 fragment.
source: Interestingly, the interaction with Ku80 (but not with Stn1) appears to be mediated through the Rif1NTE1-264 fragment, according to the Y2H analysis (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by Y2H data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The residues required for Ku80 binding are localized within the 220–240 region of Rif1 (Rif1 Ku80-binding motif, or Rif1KBM).
source: By testing several deletion constructs of the Rif1NTE1-264, we found that the residues required for Ku80 binding are localized within the 220–240 region of Rif1 (hereafter referred to as Rif1 Ku80-binding motif, or Rif1KBM) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The 220–240 region of Rif1 is fairly conserved in five species closely related to H. polymorpha.
source: This region is fairly conserved in five species closely related to H. polymorpha (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 2), and substitution of either F225 or R230 with a negatively charged glutamic acid residue abolish the Rif1NTE150-264-Ku80 interaction in the Y2H system (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Substitution of either F225 or R230 with a negatively charged glutamic acid residue abolish the Rif1NTE150-264-Ku80 interaction in the Y2H system.
source: This region is fairly conserved in five species closely related to H. polymorpha (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 2), and substitution of either F225 or R230 with a negatively charged glutamic acid residue abolish the Rif1NTE150-264-Ku80 interaction in the Y2H system (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Y2H data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Rif1-Ku interaction can be observed in vivo by Co-IP experiments.
source: Rif1-Ku interaction can also be observed in vivo by Co-IP experiments (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Deletion of either KU80 or KU70 led to a ~ 4 fold reduction in Rif1-HA telomere occupancy.
source: Deletion of either KU80 or KU70 led to a ~ 4 fold reduction in Rif1-HA telomere occupancy (Figure 5E), consistent with the idea that binding to Ku is important for Rif1 telomere association.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Binding to Ku is important for Rif1 telomere association.
source: Deletion of either KU80 or KU70 led to a ~ 4 fold reduction in Rif1-HA telomere occupancy (Figure 5E), consistent with the idea that binding to Ku is important for Rif1 telomere association.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP data showing reduced Rif1 binding in Ku deletion strains (Figure 5E).

claim: Rif1NTE1-264 fragments with either F225E or R230E mutation were unable to localize to telomeres.
source: In agreement with the Y2H data, Rif1NTE1-264 fragments with either F225E or R230E mutation were unable to localize to telomeres (Figure 5F and G), confirming that Rif1NTE-Ku80 interaction does occur in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data (Figure 5F) and Western blot data (Figure 5G).

claim: Rif1NTE-Ku80 interaction does occur in vivo.
source: In agreement with the Y2H data, Rif1NTE1-264 fragments with either F225E or R230E mutation were unable to localize to telomeres (Figure 5F and G), confirming that Rif1NTE-Ku80 interaction does occur in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined Y2H and ChIP data (Figure 5C, F, G).

claim: F225E and R230E substitutions did not affect the ability of the full-length Rif1 to bind telomeric DNA.
source: However, F225E and R230E substitutions did not affect the ability of the full-length Rif1 to bind telomeric DNA (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Double mutation F225E/R230E and substitution of amino acids 225–230 with alanines (the 6A mutant) did not perturb Rif1 telomere binding.
source: Double mutation F225E/R230E and substitution of amino acids 225–230 with alanines (the 6A mutant) also did not perturb Rif1 telomere binding (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Neither F225E/R230E nor 6A mutation led to a noticeable telomere length increase.
source: Moreover, neither mutation led to a noticeable telomere length increase (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Rif1 contains other sites for Ku binding which are more important in vivo than Rif1NTE-Ku80 interaction.
source: Thus, Rif1 contains other sites for Ku binding which are more important in vivo than Rif1NTE-Ku80 interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutations in Rif1KBM do not affect full-length Rif1 telomere binding or function (Figure 5H, I).

claim: Telomeric DNA is co-immunoprecipitated with Ku.
source: To verify this, we performed ChIP experiments with the Ku70-HA and Ku80-HA strains, which showed that telomeric DNA is co-immunoprecipitated with Ku (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Deletion of either Ku component perturbs telomere length maintenance.
source: Moreover, deletion of either Ku component perturbs telomere length maintenance (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), confirming that Ku heterodimer is indeed a part of telomeric chromatin in H. polymorpha.

claim: Ku heterodimer is a part of telomeric chromatin in H. polymorpha.
source: Moreover, deletion of either Ku component perturbs telomere length maintenance (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), confirming that Ku heterodimer is indeed a part of telomeric chromatin in H. polymorpha.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP and telomere length data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).

claim: Deletion of RIF1 leads to only ~2 fold reduction in Ku80 occupancy.

evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Rif1 is more reliant on the Ku's presence at telomeres than Ku on Rif1's.
source: Deletion of RIF1 leads to only ~2 fold reduction in Ku80 occupancy (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), in agreement with the idea that Rif1 is more reliant on the Ku's presence at telomeres than Ku on Rif1's.
evidence: This is inferred from the asymmetric effects of Rif1 and Ku deletions on each other's telomere occupancy (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Ku loss leads to telomere shortening (~25–50% reduction in telomere length).
source: However, Ku loss leads to telomere shortening (~25–50% reduction in telomere length, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Figure 5J), indicating to a positive role of Ku in telomere lengthening.
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and Figure 5J.

claim: Ku has a positive role in telomere lengthening.
source: However, Ku loss leads to telomere shortening (~25–50% reduction in telomere length, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Figure 5J), indicating to a positive role of Ku in telomere lengthening.
evidence: This is inferred from the telomere shortening observed in Ku deletion strains (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Figure 5J).

claim: TER knock-out resulted in ~40% reduction in telomere length.

claim: Rif1-HA telomere occupancy diminished only ~2 fold in TER knock-out strain.
source: TER knock-out resulted in ~40% reduction in telomere length, whereas Rif1-HA telomere occupancy diminished only ~2 fold (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D, E); contrasting to ~4 fold Rif1 ChIP signal drop in case of Ku mutants (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Inhibition of telomerase by Rif1 is attenuated in the absence of Ku.
source: Interestingly, RIF1 deletion in a ∆ku80 background does not lead to strong telomere elongation compared to the parental ∆ku80 strain, suggesting that inhibition of telomerase by Rif1 is attenuated in the absence of Ku (Figure 5J).

source: These results suggest that Ku potentially recruits some telomere addition factor, while the Rif1 fragment may compete with this putative factor for Ku80 binding.

source: In S. cerevisiae, Ku is one of the accessory subunits of telomerase stably bound to its RNA component.
evidence: This is established knowledge about S. cerevisiae telomerase.

claim: HpKu is not a stable telomerase component.

evidence: This is inferred from the RNA Co-IP data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).

claim: The Rif1-Stn1 interaction is DNA-independent.
source: Benzonase treatment of the extracts prior to the IP does not diminish the amount of co-precipitated Stn1 (Figure 6A), suggesting that the Rif1-Stn1 interaction is DNA-independent.
evidence: This is inferred from the Co-IP data with benzonase treatment (Figure 6A).

claim: Stn1 is essential for cell viability (as two other components of the CST complex – Cdc13 and Ten1).
source: We were unable to test the effect of the STN1 knockout on the Rif1 telomere binding, since Stn1 is essential for cell viability (as two other components of the CST complex – Cdc13 and Ten1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by random spore analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Stn1∆C381-Flag and Stn1∆C221-Flag strains have greatly elongated telomeres.
source: C-terminal truncations in Stn1 are well tolerated by cells, although the Stn1∆C381-Flag and Stn1∆C221-Flag strains have greatly elongated telomeres (Figure 6D), similar to the Stn1 truncation mutants in S. cerevisiae (Petreaca et al., 2007; Petreaca et al., 2006; Puglisi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 6D and citations to Petreaca et al., 2007; Petreaca et al., 2006; Puglisi et al., 2008.

claim: Rif1 telomere association is reduced in the strains with stn1 C-terminal truncation mutations, although the reduction is relatively modest (~2.5 fold).
source: Rif1 telomere association is reduced in the strains with these stn1 mutations, although the reduction is relatively modest (~2.5 fold, Figure 6E).

claim: It is Rif1 that recruits Stn1 to telomeres, and not vice versa.
source: Interestingly, we found that Stn1 telomere binding is completely abolished upon RIF1 deletion, suggesting that it is actually Rif1 that recruits Stn1 to telomeres, and not vice versa (Figure 6F).

claim: Stn1 telomere occupancy is diminished (~2 fold) in the ∆ku80 strain.

source: Remarkably, the existence of a physical interaction between Rif1 and the CST complex was proposed (but not demonstrated experimentally) in a study by Anbalagan et al., 2011 to explain the specific requirement of Rif1 for viability of S. cerevisiae cells with hypomorphic mutations in Cdc13 and Stn1.

claim: The N-terminal extension (NTE) of Rif1 is an accessory domain partially promoting Rif1 telomeric localization in H. polymorpha.
source: We demonstrated that the N-terminal extension (NTE) of Rif1 is an accessory domain partially promoting Rif1 telomeric localization in H. polymorpha.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented (Figures 1, 3, 4).

claim: DNA binding by Rif1NTE is weak and lacks clearly defined specificity toward a particular telomeric substrate.
source: Given that DNA binding by Rif1NTE is weak and lacks clearly defined specificity toward a particular telomeric substrate, we believe that it may simply stabilize Rif1 at telomeres, while the preference for the telomeric chromatin is provided by the ability to contact Ku heterodimer.
evidence: This is based on the EMSA data showing weak and non-specific DNA binding (Figure 3).
